priorities.topic: World Cup 2026 and American Transit: How Host Cities Are (and Aren't) Prepared
priorities.angle: The 2026 FIFA World Cup kicked off this month with matches across 11 US cities. Examine how transit agencies in Los Angeles, New York, Dallas, Seattle, Miami, and others planned (or failed to plan) for sudden ridership surges — covering special service expansions, fare policy, coordination failures, and what lessons will remain after the tournament ends.
priorities.rationale: Highest-timeliness news hook of the week. World Cup 2026 is actively happening in US cities right now. Streetsblog covered World Cup fan travel today. This is a direct hook to real-world transit stress-testing that no other piece in our archive touches. High search-traffic window while matches continue.

priorities.topic: Census Data Blackout: What the Federal Noise Infusion Ban Means for Transit Planning
priorities.angle: The Census Bureau just banned noise infusion from statistical products (top Hacker News story today). Transit agencies rely on Census ACS data for route planning, Title VI equity analysis, and FTA grant applications. Analyze what data products are affected, how planners currently use them, and what workarounds or risks emerge from this policy shift.
priorities.rationale: Direct hook from today's top HN story. Noise infusion ban is a policy change with concrete downstream consequences for transit planning — a niche audience (transit planners, data analysts, equity advocates) will search this intersection. Nobody else will have covered this angle today.

priorities.topic: The First and Last Mile Problem: Why Transit Fails at the Edges
priorities.angle: Explain why the 'first/last mile' gap — the distance between where transit ends and where people need to go — is the single biggest barrier to transit adoption in American cities. Cover: walking radius research, bike/scooter integration programs, demand-responsive feeders, and the suburban design problem. Include examples from LA, Houston, and Minneapolis.
priorities.rationale: Evergreen foundational topic not covered in our archive. Highly searchable. The Streetsblog sprawl-and-youth-opportunity story today, and the greenways-funding-shortfall story, both point to this gap in coverage. Pairs naturally with existing TOD and transit desert content.

priorities.topic: The Hidden Math of Fare Evasion: Why Crackdowns Often Cost More Than They Collect
priorities.angle: Walk through the actual economics of fare evasion enforcement — enforcement officer salaries, court costs, reduced ridership from hostile enforcement, vs. actual fare recovery rates. Compare NYC, DC Metro, and LA Metro approaches. Build to the policy question: is proof-of-payment or honor-system cheaper than paid barriers?
priorities.rationale: New script topic not yet in the backlog. Fare evasion is politically charged and widely searched — 'fare evasion crackdown' stories appear weekly. The economics angle is counterintuitive (crackdowns can be net negative) which drives shares and engagement. Complements existing fare structure article in docs/.
